a: A detective's evidence board pinning together clues from every camera, door log and alarm in the building.
e: A SIEM collects and correlates; it detects but does not respond on its own.

a: The 24/7 security control room where analysts watch the screens and respond to alarms.
e: The SOC is people and process; SIEM and SOAR are their tools.

a: A robot assistant that runs the SOC's playbooks automatically the moment an alarm fires.
e: SOAR acts on alerts with automated playbooks; a SIEM only detects them.

a: A flight recorder and bodyguard on every laptop, recording behavior and isolating the machine if needed.
e: EDR watches behavior on hosts and can isolate them, unlike signature-only antivirus.

a: EDR's bodyguards linked by radio with guards at the email gateway, network and cloud.
e: XDR correlates endpoint, network, email and cloud telemetry in one vendor platform.

a: The fire department's drill: detect the smoke, contain the fire, put it out, then learn why it started.
e: IR phases: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.

a: A guard who knows everyone's routine and notices when the accountant logs in at 3 AM from abroad.
e: UEBA learns normal behavior and flags deviations, catching insiders and stolen accounts.

a: A neighborhood watch group text, where organizations instantly share descriptions of new burglars.
e: AIS is CISA's free program, built on STIX and TAXII.

a: The delivery truck carrying threat-intel packages between organizations over HTTPS.
e: TAXII moves the intel; STIX is the language the intel is written in.

a: A common language for describing attackers, so every organization's intel reads the same way.
e: STIX describes threat intelligence; TAXII is how it is shared.

a: The library catalog that takes each CVE ID and adds severity scores, product lists and fix notes.
e: CVE names the flaw; the NVD adds CVSS scores and affected product details.

a: An apartment inside a building: a full home that shares the building's foundation and plumbing.
e: VMs share a hypervisor, so VM escape is the key isolation risk.

a: Your desk lives in the data center; your laptop is just a window onto it.
e: VDI keeps data in the data center, so a lost laptop leaks nothing.

a: Renting empty land with utilities hooked up — you build and maintain everything on it.
e: In IaaS you patch the OS and apps; the provider secures the hardware.

a: Eating at a restaurant: you just order, the kitchen and dishes are someone else's problem.
e: In SaaS you still own your data, user access and configuration.

a: A chaperone standing between employees and cloud apps, enforcing company rules on what's shared.
e: A CASB brings visibility and DLP to cloud apps, including unsanctioned shadow IT.

a: Hiring a professional security company to guard your building instead of training your own guards.
e: An MSSP delivers SOC-style monitoring as a service; accountability still stays with you.

a: The front desk you actually talk to — web pages, email, and DNS lookups live here.
e: Layer 7 is where WAFs, proxies and most attacks against apps operate.

a: The translator and envelope-sealer, handling encoding, compression and encryption.
e: Layer 6 converts data formats; TLS is commonly mapped here for the exam.

a: The meeting organizer who opens, keeps alive, and closes the conversation between apps.
e: Layer 5 manages sessions; it is where session hijacking concepts live.

a: The shipping department choosing registered mail (TCP) or quick postcards (UDP) and labeling the door number.
e: Layer 4 adds ports and reliability; stateful firewalls track it.

a: The postal routing system, reading IP addresses to move packets between cities.
e: Layer 3 routes between networks; routers and IP addresses live here.

a: The hallway mail carrier in one building, delivering by MAC address door to door.
e: Layer 2 moves frames locally; ARP spoofing and VLAN hopping attack here.

a: The roads themselves — copper, fiber and radio waves carrying raw bits.
e: Layer 1 attacks are physical: wiretaps, jamming, cut cables.
